analysis.title: ~12 GW US Data Center Pipeline Through 2030 at Risk in Texas and Ohio
key_insights: About 12.4 GW of cumulative US data center capacity through 2030 is at risk of delay or cancellation in Texas and Ohio after both states flipped from a Republican to a Democratic governor in the midterms. That is 4% of 2028 and 7% of 2029 cumulative capacity estimates, and 8% of the 152 GW 2030 base case.
The at-risk capacity excludes projects under construction, which Morgan Stanley expects to proceed. 2027 capacity under construction is not affected.
Incremental capacity at risk is 4.9 GW in 2028 (20% of that year's additions), 3.8 GW in 2029 (17%) and 3.7 GW in 2030 (19%).
Morgan Stanley expects governors to set requirements new data center projects must meet, which may delay rather than reduce data center volumes.

The 12.4 GW figure is an upper bound. Partisan alignment (Republican-led Texas legislature) and limits on gubernatorial authority will restrict how many campaign proposals get implemented. Total capacity estimates are unchanged at 152 GW base, 177 GW bull and 131 GW bear for 2030.

A Texas governor can issue an executive order pausing new projects until the legislature sets guidelines, make appointments to the PUCT (6-year terms coming up in 2027), and direct agencies on permitting. Governor-elect Hinojosa has advocated a moratorium on new permits until laws pass, not applying to projects under construction.

Tax changes such as ending the sales-tax exemption, local power to reject projects, codified ratepayer protections and union hiring requirements all need approval from the Republican-controlled Texas legislature.

The capacity model is a probability-weighted expected value with a 30% haircut in the base case and historical execution rates applied, so exposure sits below the broader announced pipeline. Some announced projects (e.g. certain ERCOT Batch Zero) may not be in the 451 Research dataset.

Morgan Stanley sees a slower or more restrictive approval environment as positive for incumbent colocation operators' pricing power. EQIX (Overweight, Top Pick) has nine operating Texas facilities (~3% of 280 global data centers). DLR (Equal-weight) has Dallas at 4.2% of annualized rent as of 3Q26 and an 80 MW, $300 million Digital Garland project in Texas exposed to ERCOT's verification process.
EQIX and DLR shares have shown higher beta to AI-related headline volatility, a risk of short-term price swings. Industry view is In-Line.

market_movers.rationale: Texas and Ohio delays should help incumbent colo pricing power, and EQIX has limited Texas exposure (nine facilities). The base-case valuation is $1,250 at ~24.8x forward adjusted EBITDA.

A slower approval environment could raise the scarcity value of DLR's power-secured assets, but Dallas rent exposure (4.2%) and the Digital Garland project carry regulatory risk. The base-case valuation is $215.

sector_views.rationale: Industry view In-Line. Positive on incumbent colocation operators' pricing power if Texas and Ohio approvals slow.

earnings_insights: EQIX model FY26E: ~12.4% y/y revenue growth, 51.3% adjusted EBITDA margin, ~14.8% AFFO/share growth (Morgan Stanley estimates, not reported). Morgan Stanley FY26E AFFO/share $43.00 vs consensus $44.14 (the report prints other values of 43.99 and 43.44 without labels).

DLR model FY26E: ~19.8% y/y revenue growth, 52.5% adjusted EBITDA margin, ~19.6% AFFO/share growth (Morgan Stanley estimates, not reported). Morgan Stanley FY26E FFO/share $7.92 vs consensus $8.87 (other values 8.87 and 8.31 printed without labels).
EQIX capex: $4,311mm in Dec 2025, with estimates of $5,975mm Dec 2026e, $5,900mm Dec 2027e and $6,208mm Dec 2028e.
risk_factors: Texas or Ohio governors could pause or delay new data center projects, and legislation could add tax changes, local veto power, ratepayer protections or union hiring requirements.
Macroeconomic softness reducing IT infrastructure spending.
Power density requirements higher than expected raising obsolescence risk.
Interest rates staying higher for longer.
The role of inference in colocation data centers remains uncertain.
EQIX and DLR show higher beta to AI-related headline volatility.

tension_points.bull_case: Governor-driven delays and tighter approvals reduce new supply, raising the scarcity value and pricing power of incumbent colo operators such as EQIX and DLR.
tension_points.bear_case: A moratorium, tax changes ending the sales-tax exemption, local veto power and ratepayer rules could cancel rather than delay up to 12.4 GW, and EQIX and DLR shares carry high beta to AI headlines.
tension_points.what_invalidates: A Republican-led Texas legislature acting quickly on guidelines would limit a pause to a number of months, and projects under construction proceed regardless.
